parts.description: A stainless-steel spoon with a rounded reflective bowl and a light wooden handle. The handle has visible grain, rounded edges, and metal rivets fastening it to the steel tang.
parts.reasoning: The object appears to be a composite utensil: a thin stainless-steel spoon head/tang joined to a rounded wooden handle with two metal rivets. With no product data available, dimensions are estimated at roughly 0.23-0.26 m long, 0.045-0.055 m wide at the bowl, and 0.015-0.025 m thick at the handle/bowl curvature. A plausible mass is about 0.065 kg: approximately 20-25 g of hardwood handle material plus 35-45 g of stainless steel bowl, tang, and rivets. The root-level material is set to wood because the wooden handle is the largest external/contact surface, although the metal parts likely dominate a substantial fraction of the mass. The density value of 650 kg/m^3 represents typical finished hardwood and is suitable as the dominant-material density; the explicit mass should be used for accurate rigid-body behavior because the composite steel/wood construction is not represented by one uniform density. Wood-on-common-surfaces static friction is typically 0.4-0.6, so 0.52 static and 0.38 dynamic are appropriate effective values; polished steel portions would be lower, but the handle contact area and rounded wood surface justify a wood-dominant coefficient. Restitution is modest at 0.32 because the object is lightweight but not elastomeric; impacts will be slightly lively due to the steel bowl, but the wooden handle and thin geometry dissipate energy. For collision, convex decomposition is recommended over a single convex hull because a single hull would overfill the concave spoon bowl and the narrow neck/handle transition. A small set of convexes should approximate the wooden rounded handle, steel tang/neck, and spoon bowl rim/shell; if bowl concavity is critical for containing small objects, an SDF mesh can be used at higher cost, but convex decomposition is a better dynamic rigid-body default in Isaac Sim/PhysX. Contact offset is set to 2 mm to improve contact generation for the thin metal bowl and rounded edges, with a near-zero rest offset to avoid visible hovering. CCD is enabled because the spoon has thin sheet-metal regions that can tunnel through surfaces during drops or fast manipulation. For stable contact stacking, 120 Hz simulation is recommended; velocity should generally be initialized at zero and kept within ordinary rigid-body limits, with sleep/hibernation enabled in the scene for performance when the spoon comes to rest. Compliant contacts are disabled because the model is treated as a rigid non-deformable composite, though a very high stiffness/low damping compliance could be added only if contact jitter appears on the thin rim.
